newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court rejects Corea suit in Scientology row.
newsitem.headline: German court rejects Corea suit in Scientology row.

text.p: A German court on Thursday ruled against Chick Corea in a discrimination suit the American jazz pianist had brought against the southwestern German state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.

An administrative court in Mannheim said Baden-Wuerttemberg had not violated Corea's basic rights when it decreed in 1993 that state funds could not be used for concerts in which members of the Church of Scientology appeared.
A spokeswoman for the Church of Scientology in Hamburg denounced the court's ruling, saying that banning state funds because Corea is a Scientologist was discriminatory.
"He felt that he was being discriminated against because of his religious beliefs," said Gisela Hackenjos, a spokeswoman for the Church of Scientology. "His basic human rights were being violated."
But in a brief statement the state court ruled that the Baden-Wuerttemberg Ministry for Cultural affairs did not discriminate against Corea with its threat to withhold funding.
"Neither the honour of the plaintiff nor his basic rights were violated by the state," the court said. It will provide a detailed written explanation within the next few weeks.

The ministry had issued a decree on July 9, 1993 that said: "State subsidies for an event can be called into question when self-professed members of the Scientologists or other similar groups appear."

Hackenjos said Corea had been appearing in concerts in Germany for many years and had continued to perform here even after the state funding ban was announced. She said he does not mention the Church of Scientology during his concerts.

Scientology, founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard, gives would-be members personality tests and then offers courses and literature to help them realise what the church sees as their full potential.

In Germany, which has stricter regulations on church status than the United States and has refused to register Scientology as a religion, some officials see it as a totalitarian group using manipulative practices for profit.
Because of its own Nazi past, Germany tends to take a tough stand on groups it thinks threaten its postwar democracy.

The youth wing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democratic (CDU) called earlier this year for a boycott of the Hollywood blockbuster "Mission:Impossible" because it stars Tom Cruise -- one of several high-profile Scientologists.
Scientology last week blasted recent moves to limit its activities in Germany, saying in an advertisement in the New York Times that Bonn used Nazi-style tactics against it.
Bonn rejected that charge as absurd and said it insulted the millions of Jewish victims of the Nazi Holocaust.
